[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Nobel2008Economics_news_conference1.jpg/250px-Nobel2008Economics_news_conference1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobel2008Economics_news_conference1.jpg)

The announcement of the 2008 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in Nobel Prize Press Conference. The laureate of the Prize was [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman").

The **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences**, officially the **Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-3) ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Sveriges riksbanks pris i ekonomisk vetenskap till Alfred Nobels minne_), commonly referred to as the **Nobel Prize in Economics**, is an award in the field of [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeSelectionProcess-4)

The first Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded in 1969 to [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch") and [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-Winners1969-5) Each recipient receives a [medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma") and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-6) In 1969, Frisch and Tinbergen were given a combined 375,000 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), which is equivalent to 2,871,041 SEK in December 2007. The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-7)

As of the awarding of the 2023 prize, 55 Prizes in Economic Sciences have been given to 93 individuals.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelLaureatesList-8) As of October 2023, the department of economics with the most affiliated [laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate") in economic sciences is the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-10) with 16 affiliated laureates. As of 2023, the institutions with the most [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") (or equivalent) graduates who went on to receive the prize are Harvard University and MIT (13 each), followed by the University of Chicago (10). As of 2024, the institutions with the most affiliated faculty at the time of the award are the University of Chicago (15), followed by MIT (10), then by Princeton University and Harvard University (8 each).

**Sir John Richard Hicks** (8 April 1904 – 20 May 1989) was a British [economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economist "Economist"). He is considered one of the most important and influential economists of the twentieth century. The most familiar of his many contributions in the field of [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") were his statement of [consumer demand theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_theory "Consumer theory") in [microeconomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microeconomics "Microeconomics"), and the [IS–LM model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IS%E2%80%93LM_model "IS–LM model") (1937), which summarised a [Keynesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynesian "Keynesian") view of [macroeconomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroeconomics "Macroeconomics"). His book _[Value and Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value\_and\_Capital "Value and Capital")_ (1939) significantly extended [general-equilibrium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_equilibrium_theory "General equilibrium theory") and value theory. The [compensated demand function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compensated_demand_function "Compensated demand function") is named the Hicksian demand function in memory of him.

In 1972 he received the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") (jointly) for his pioneering contributions to [general equilibrium theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_equilibrium_theory "General equilibrium theory") and [welfare theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_economics "Welfare economics").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-3)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Hicks&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Hicks was born in 1904 in [Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warwick "Warwick"), England, and was the son of Edward Hicks, editor and part proprietor of the Warwick and Leamington Spa Courier newspaper, and Dorothy Catherine, née Stephens, daughter of a non-conformist minister.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-5)

He was educated at [Clifton College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton_College "Clifton College") (1917–1922)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-6) and at [Balliol College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balliol_College,_Oxford "Balliol College, Oxford") (1922–1926), and was financed by mathematical scholarships. During his school days and in his first year at Oxford, he specialised in mathematics but also had interests in literature and history. In 1923, he moved to [Philosophy, Politics and Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy,_Politics_and_Economics "Philosophy, Politics and Economics"), the "new school" that was just being started at Oxford. He graduated with [second-class honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_undergraduate_degree_classification "British undergraduate degree classification") and, as he stated, "no adequate qualification in any of the subjects" that he had studied.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Hicks&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

From 1926 to 1935, Hicks lectured at the [London School of Economics and Political Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-lse-8) He started as a labour economist and did descriptive work on industrial relations but gradually, he moved over to the analytical side, where his mathematics background returned to the fore. Hicks's influences included [Lionel Robbins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Robbins "Lionel Robbins") and such associates as [Friedrich von Hayek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_von_Hayek "Friedrich von Hayek"), [R.G.D. Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R.G.D._Allen "R.G.D. Allen"), [Nicholas Kaldor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Kaldor "Nicholas Kaldor"), [Abba Lerner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abba_Lerner "Abba Lerner") and [Ursula Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Ursula_Hicks "Lady Ursula Hicks"), the last of whom, in 1935, became his wife.

From 1935 to 1938, he lectured at [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University "Cambridge University") where he was also a fellow of [Gonville & Caius College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonville_and_Caius_College,_Cambridge "Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge"). He was occupied mainly in writing _Value and Capital_, which was based on his earlier work in London. From 1938 to 1946, he was Professor at the [University of Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Manchester "University of Manchester"). There, he did his main work on welfare economics, with its application to social accounting.

In 1946, he returned to [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University "Oxford University"), first as a research fellow of [Nuffield College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuffield_College,_Oxford "Nuffield College, Oxford") (1946–1952) then as [Drummond Professor of Political Economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drummond_Professor_of_Political_Economy "Drummond Professor of Political Economy") (1952–1965) and finally as a research fellow of [All Souls College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Souls_College "All Souls College") (1965–1971), where he continued writing after his retirement.

## Later life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Hicks&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

Hicks was knighted in 1964 and became an honorary fellow of [Linacre College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linacre_College "Linacre College"). He was co-recipient of the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences (with [Kenneth J. Arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_J._Arrow "Kenneth J. Arrow")) in 1972. He donated the Nobel Prize to the [London School of Economics and Political Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics")'s Library Appeal in 1973.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-lse-8) He died on 20 May 1989 at his home in the [Cotswold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotswold "Cotswold") village of [Blockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockley "Blockley").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-9)

Hicks's early work as a [labour economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_economics "Labour economics") culminated in _[The Theory of Wages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Theory\_of\_Wages "The Theory of Wages")_ (1932, 2nd ed. 1963), still considered standard in the field. He collaborated with R.G.D. Allen in two seminal papers on [value theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_theory "Value theory") published in 1934.

His [magnum opus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterpiece "Masterpiece") is _[Value and Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value\_and\_Capital "Value and Capital")_ published in 1939. The book built on [ordinal utility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_utility "Ordinal utility") and mainstreamed the now-standard distinction between the [substitution effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substitution_effect "Substitution effect") and the [income effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Income_effect "Income effect") for an individual in [demand theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_theory "Consumer theory") for the 2-good case. It generalised the analysis to the case of one good and a [composite good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composite_good "Composite good"), that is, all other goods. It aggregated individuals and businesses through demand and supply across the economy. It anticipated the [aggregation problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aggregation_problem "Aggregation problem"), most acutely for the stock of capital goods. It introduced [general equilibrium theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_equilibrium_theory "General equilibrium theory") to an English-speaking audience, refined the theory for dynamic analysis, and for the first time attempted a rigorous statement of stability conditions for general equilibrium. In the course of analysis Hicks formalised [comparative statics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparative_statics "Comparative statics"). In the same year, he also developed the famous "compensation" criterion called [Kaldor–Hicks efficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaldor%E2%80%93Hicks_efficiency "Kaldor–Hicks efficiency") for welfare comparisons of alternative public policies or economic states.

Hicks's most familiar contribution in [macroeconomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroeconomics "Macroeconomics") was the [Hicks–Hansen IS–LM model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IS%E2%80%93LM_model "IS–LM model"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-10) published in his paper "[Mr. Keynes and the "Classics"; a suggested interpretation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr_Keynes_and_the_Classics "Mr Keynes and the Classics")". This model formalised an interpretation of the theory of [John Maynard Keynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Maynard_Keynes "John Maynard Keynes") (see [Keynesian economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynesian_economics "Keynesian economics")), and describes the economy as a balance between three commodities: money, consumption and investment. Hicks himself wavered in his acceptance of his IS–LM formulation; in a paper published in 1980 he dismissed it as a 'classroom gadget'.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-11)

## Contributions to interpretation of income for accounting purposes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Hicks&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Contributions to interpretation of income for accounting purposes")]

Hicks's influential discourse on [income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profit_(accounting) "Profit (accounting)") sets the basis for its subjectivity but relevancy for accounting purposes. He aptly summarized it as follows. "The purpose of income calculations in practical affairs is to give people an indication of the amount they can consume without impoverishing themselves".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-academia.edu-12)

Formally, he defined income precisely in three measures:

**Hicks's number 1 measure of income**: "the maximum amount, which can be spent during a period if there is to be an expectation of maintaining intact the capital value of prospective receipts (in money terms)" (Hicks, 1946, p.173)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-academia.edu-12)

**Hicks's number 2 measure of income** (market price-neutral): "the maximum amount the individual can spend during a week, and still expect to be able to spend the same amount in each ensuing week" (Hicks, 1946, p.174).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-academia.edu-12)

**Hicks's number 3 measure of income** (takes into account market prices): "the maximum amount of money which an individual can spend this week, and still expect to be able to spend the same amount in real terms in each ensuing week" (Hicks, 1946, p.174)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hicks#cite_note-academia.edu-12)

**James Edward Meade**[FBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow_of_the_British_Academy "Fellow of the British Academy") (23 June 1907 – 22 December 1995) was a British [economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economist "Economist") who made major contributions to the theory of [international trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_trade "International trade") and [welfare economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_economics "Welfare economics").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-3) Along with [Richard Kahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kahn,_Baron_Kahn "Richard Kahn, Baron Kahn"), James Meade helped develop the concept of the [Keynesian multiplier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keynesian_multiplier "Keynesian multiplier") while participating in the [Cambridge circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Circus_(economics) "Cambridge Circus (economics)"). In the 1930s, he served as specialist adviser on behalf of the British government at the [Economic and Financial Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_and_Financial_Organization_of_the_League_of_Nations "Economic and Financial Organization of the League of Nations") of the [League of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Nations "League of Nations").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-ClavinWessels-4):477

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Meade&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Born in [Swanage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swanage "Swanage"), Meade was brought up in [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset"), and educated at [Lambrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambrook "Lambrook") prep school, [Malvern College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malvern_College "Malvern College"), and [Oriel College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriel_College,_Oxford "Oriel College, Oxford"), where he initially read [classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literae_humaniores "Literae humaniores"), before switching (in 1928) to the newly-established course in [philosophy, politics, and economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy,_politics_and_economics "Philosophy, politics and economics").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-5) He was elected a Fellow of [Hertford College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertford_College,_Oxford "Hertford College, Oxford") in 1930, and was a lecturer in economics at Oxford from 1931 to 1937.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-:0-6) During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), he was recalled to the Economic Section of the Secretariat of the [War Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Cabinet#Churchill_war_ministry "War Cabinet"), which he chaired from 1946 to 1947.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-:0-6)

He was appointed [CB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Bath "Order of the Bath") in 1946, and served as President of the [Royal Economic Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Economic_Society "Royal Economic Society") from 1964 to 1966.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-:0-6) While his work was not confined by political boundaries, he advised the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") in the 1930s, and was a member of the [Social Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Democratic_Party_(UK) "Social Democratic Party (UK)") during the 1980s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-:0-6) He once said that he had "my heart to the left, and my brain to the right".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-7)

In 1976 he received an Honorary Doctorate from the [University of Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bath "University of Bath").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-8)

Along with the Swedish economist [Bertil Ohlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertil_Ohlin "Bertil Ohlin"), he received the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in 1977 "for their pathbreaking contribution to the theory of [international trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_trade "International trade") and international [capital movements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_movement "Capital movement")".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-nobelprize.org-2)

In 1981 he attracted attention as one of the 364 economists who signed a letter to _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ questioning [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher")'s economic policies, warning that it would only result in deepening the prevailing [depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(economics) "Depression (economics)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meade#cite_note-11)

**Elinor Claire** "**Lin**" **Ostrom** (née **Awan**; August 7, 1933 – June 12, 2012) was an American [political scientist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science") and [political economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_economy "Political economy")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-nature-obit-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-3) whose work was associated with [New Institutional Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_institutional_economics "New institutional economics") and the resurgence of [political economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_economy "Political economy").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-4) In 2009, she was awarded the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") for her "analysis of economic governance, especially [the commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_commons "The commons")", which she shared with [Oliver E. Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_E._Williamson "Oliver E. Williamson"); she was [the first woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economics "List of Nobel Memorial Prize laureates in Economics") to win the prize.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-5)

Trained in political science at [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA "UCLA"), Ostrom was a faculty member at [Indiana University Bloomington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_University_Bloomington "Indiana University Bloomington") for 47 years. Beginning in the 1960s, Ostrom was involved in resource management policy and created a research center, the [Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomington_school "Bloomington school"), which attracted scientists from different disciplines from around the world. Working and teaching at her center was created on the principle of a workshop, rather than a university with lectures and a strict hierarchy. Late in her career, she held an affiliation with [Arizona State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_State_University "Arizona State University").

Ostrom studied the interaction of people and ecosystems for many years and showed that the use of exhaustible resources by groups of people (communities, cooperatives, trusts, trade unions) can be rational and prevent depletion of the resource without either [state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_(polity) "State (polity)") intervention or [markets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_(economics) "Market (economics)") with [private property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_property "Private property").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-6)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Elinor Claire Awan was born in [Los Angeles, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California "Los Angeles, California"), as the only child of Leah Hopkins, a musician, and Adrian Awan, a set designer.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Leonard-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-TelegraphObit-8) Her parents separated early in her life, and Elinor lived with her mother most of the time.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Wall-9) She attended a [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant "Protestant") church with her mother and often spent weekends with her father's Jewish family.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Leonard-7)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-10) Growing up in the post-Depression era to divorced artisans, Ostrom described herself as a "poor kid."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Wall-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-11) Her major recreational activity was swimming, where she eventually joined a swimming team and swam competitively until she started teaching swimming to earn funds to help put herself through college.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Elinor_Ostrom_%E2%80%93_Biographical-12)

Ostrom grew up across the street from [Beverly Hills High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Hills_High_School "Beverly Hills High School"), which she attended, graduating in 1951.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:0-13) She regarded this as fortunate, for the school had a very high rate of college admission. During Ostrom's junior year, she was encouraged to join the debate team. Learning debate tactics had an important impact on her ways of thinking. It allowed her to realize there are two sides to public policy and it is imperative to have quality arguments for both sides.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Elinor_Ostrom_%E2%80%93_Biographical-12) As a high school student, Elinor Ostrom had been discouraged from studying [trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry "Trigonometry"), as girls without top marks in [algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebra "Algebra") and [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry "Geometry") were not allowed to take the subject. No one in her immediate family had any college experience, but seeing that 90% of students in her high school attended college, she saw it as the "normal" thing to do.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Elinor_Ostrom_%E2%80%93_Biographical-12) Her mother did not wish for her to attend college, seeing no reason for it.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:0-13)

She attended UCLA, receiving a B.A. with honors in [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science") at [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") in 1954.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-NAS-14) By attending multiple summer sessions and extra classes throughout semesters, she was able to graduate in three years. She worked at the library, [dime store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dime_store "Dime store") and bookstore in order to pay her fees which were $50 per semester.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Elinor_Ostrom_%E2%80%93_Biographical-12) After graduation, she had trouble finding a job because employers presumed that she was only looking for jobs as a teacher or secretary. She began a job as an export clerk after taking a correspondence course for [shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shorthand "Shorthand"), which she later found to be helpful when taking notes in face-to-face interviews on research projects. After a year, she obtained a position as assistant personnel manager in a business firm that had never before hired a woman in anything but a secretarial position. This job inspired her to think about attending graduate-level courses and eventually applying for a research assistantship and admission to a Ph.D. program.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Elinor_Ostrom_%E2%80%93_Biographical-12)

Lacking any [math](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics") from her undergraduate education and [trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry "Trigonometry") from high school, she was consequently rejected for an [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") Ph.D. program at UCLA.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-15) She was admitted to UCLA's graduate program in [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science"), where she was awarded an M.A. in 1962 and a Ph.D. in 1965.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-NAS-14) The teams of graduate students she was involved with were analyzing the political economic effects of a group of groundwater basins in Southern California. Specifically, Ostrom was assigned to look at the West Basin. She found it is very difficult to manage a common-pool resource when it is used between individuals.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Elinor_Ostrom_%E2%80%93_Biographical-12) The locals were pumping too much groundwater and salt water seeped into the basin. Ostrom was impressed with how people from conflicting and overlapping jurisdictions who depended on that source found incentives to settle contradictions and solve the problem. She made the study of this collaboration the topic of her dissertation, laying the foundation for the study of "shared resources".

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Ostrom was informed by fieldwork, both her own and that of others. During her PhD at the University of California, Los Angeles, she spent years studying the water wars and pumping races going on in the 1950s in her own dry backyard. In contrast to the prevailing rational-economic predictions of [Malthusianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malthusianism "Malthusianism") and the [tragedy of the commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy_of_the_commons "Tragedy of the commons"), she showed cases where humans were not trapped and helpless amid diminishing supplies. In her book _[Governing the Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governing\_the\_Commons?action=edit&redlink=1 "Governing the Commons (page does not exist)")_, she draws on studies of irrigation systems in [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") and the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"), mountain villages in [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland") and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), and fisheries in [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia") and [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-16)

In 1961, [Vincent Ostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Ostrom "Vincent Ostrom"), Charles Tiebout, and Robert Warren published "The Organization of Government in Metropolitan Areas," which would go on to be an influential article and introduced themes that would be central to the Ostroms' work.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:0-13)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-17) However, the article aggravated a conflict with UCLA's Bureau of Governmental Research because, counter to the Bureau's interests, it advised against centralization of metropolitan areas in favor of [polycentrism](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/polycentric "wikt:polycentric"). This conflict prompted the Ostroms to leave UCLA.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:0-13) They moved to [Bloomington, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomington,_Indiana "Bloomington, Indiana"), in 1965, when Vincent accepted a political science professorship at Indiana University.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Woo-18) She joined the faculty as a visiting assistant professor. The first course she taught was an evening class on American government.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Leonard-7)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Zagorski-19)

Ostrom is probably best known for revisiting the so-called "[tragedy of the commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy_of_the_commons "Tragedy of the commons")" – a conjecture proposed by biologist [Garrett Hardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrett_Hardin "Garrett Hardin") in 1968.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:1-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-21)

> "In an article by the same name published in the journal Science, Hardin theorized that if each herdsman sharing a piece of common grazing land made the individually rational economic decision of increasing the number of cattle he keeps on the land, the collective effect would deplete or destroy the commons. In other words, multiple individuals—acting independently and rationally consulting their own self-interest—will ultimately deplete a shared limited resource, even when it is clear that it is not in anyone's long-term interest for this to happen. Ostrom believes that the "tragedy" in such situations isn't inevitable, as Hardin thought. Instead, if the herders decide to cooperate with one another, monitoring each other's use of the land and enforcing rules for managing it, they can avoid the tragedy."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:1-20)

[Garrett Hardin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrett_Hardin "Garrett Hardin") believes that the most important aspect that we need to realize today is the need to abandon the principle of shared resources in reproduction. A possible alternative to the [tragedy of the commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tragedy_of_the_commons "Tragedy of the commons") (shared needs) was described in Elinor Ostrom's book _Governing the Commons_. Based on her fieldwork, the book demonstrates that there are practical algorithms for the collective use of a limited common resource, which solve the many issues with both government/regulation driven solutions and market-based ones.

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/90/SPEA.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPEA.jpg)

[School of Public and Environmental Affairs at Indiana University Bloomington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Public_and_Environmental_Affairs "School of Public and Environmental Affairs"), where Ostrom taught.

In 1973, Ostrom and her husband founded the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis at Indiana University.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-22) Examining the use of [collective action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_action "Collective action"), [trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trust_(sociology) "Trust (sociology)"), and [cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperation "Cooperation") in the management of [common pool resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_pool_resources "Common pool resources") (CPR), her institutional approach to public policy, known as the [Institutional analysis and development framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutional_analysis_and_development_framework "Institutional analysis and development framework") (IAD), has been considered sufficiently distinct to be thought of as a separate school of [public choice theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_choice_theory "Public choice theory").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-23) She authored many books in the fields of [organizational theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organizational_theory "Organizational theory"), [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science"), and [public administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_administration "Public administration"). Elinor Ostrom was a dedicated scholar until the very end of her life. Indeed, on the day before she died, she sent e-mail messages to at least two different sets of coauthors about papers that she was writing with them. She was the chief scientific advisor for the International Council for Science (ICSU) Planet Under Pressure meeting in London in March, and [Johan Rockström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Rockstr%C3%B6m "Johan Rockström") of the Stockholm Resilience Centre wrote that

> "Lin, up until the very end, was heavily involved in our preparations for the Nobel laureate dialogues on global sustainability we will be hosting in Rio 17th and 18th of June during the UN Rio+20 Earth Summit. In the end, she decided she could not come in person, but was contributing sharp, enthusiastically charged, inputs, in the way only she could."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Arrow_13135%E2%80%9313136-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-25)

It was long unanimously held among economists that natural resources that were collectively used by their users would be over-exploited and destroyed in the long-term. Elinor Ostrom disproved this idea by conducting field studies on how people in small, local communities manage shared natural resources, such as pastures, fishing waters and forests. She showed that when natural resources are jointly used by their users, in time, rules are established for how these are to be cared for and they become used in a way that is both economically and ecologically sustainable.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-26)

Ostrom was appointed Professor of Political Science in 1974. She was the head of the department from 1980 to 1984, and then held the Arthur F. Bentley Chair of Political Science[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-27) She was appointed Distinguished Professor in 2010 and held a partial appointment in the [School of Public and Environmental Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Public_and_Environmental_Affairs "School of Public and Environmental Affairs").

She was senior research director of the Vincent and Elinor Ostrom Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, Distinguished Professor and Arthur F. Bentley Professor of Political Science in the College of Arts and Sciences, and professor in the School of Public and Environmental Affairs.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-auto-28) The Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis was meant to utilize diverse scholars throughout economics, political science, and other fields to collaborate and attempt to understand how institutional arrangements in a diverse set of ecological and social economic political settings affected behavior and outcomes. The goal was not to fly around the world collecting data, rather it is to create a network of scholars who live in particular areas of the world and had strong interests in forest conditions and forest policy conducted the studies.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-29)

Ostrom's innovative and ground-breaking research was supported by [National Science Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Science_Foundation "National Science Foundation"), the [Andrew Mellon Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_W._Mellon_Foundation "Andrew W. Mellon Foundation"), the Hynde and Harry Bradley Foundation, the [MacArthur Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Foundation "MacArthur Foundation"), the [Ford Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Foundation "Ford Foundation"), the [Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization "Food and Agriculture Organization"), U.S.A.I.D., the [U.S. Geological Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Geological_Survey "United States Geological Survey"), the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice"), and the [National Institute of Mental Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Mental_Health "National Institute of Mental Health").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:2-30)

Ostrom has been involved in international activities throughout her long and productive career. She had experience in Kenya, Nepal and Nigeria, and also made research trips to Australia, [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia "Bolivia"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), Indonesia, Mexico, [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"), [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland") and [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"). During workshops and research grants, she and her husband supported many international students, and visited researchers and policymakers. They did not have children of their own and used personal funds and efforts to receive grants to help others. In a 2010 interview, Ostrom noted that because they had no family to support, "I was not ever concerned about salary, so that's never been an issue for me. For some colleagues who have big families, and all the rest, it's a major issue."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:2-30)

Ostrom was a founding member and first president of the [IASC (International Association for the Study of the Commons)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_for_the_Study_of_the_Commons "International Association for the Study of the Commons").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-31) She was a lead researcher for the Sustainable Agriculture and Natural Resource Management Collaborative Research Support Program (SANREM CRSP), managed by [Virginia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Tech "Virginia Tech") and funded by [USAID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USAID "USAID").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Researcher_for_Virginia_Tech_program_wins_Nobel_Prize-32) Beginning in 2008, she and her husband [Vincent Ostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Ostrom "Vincent Ostrom") advised the journal _Transnational Corporations Review_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-33)

## Research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Research")]

Ostrom's early work emphasized the role of public choice on decisions influencing the production of public goods and services.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-34) Among her better known works in this area is her study on the polycentricity of police functions in [Indianapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis "Indianapolis").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-35) Caring for the commons had to be a multiple task, organised from the ground up and shaped to cultural norms. It had to be discussed face to face, and based on trust. Dr. Ostrom, besides poring over satellite data and quizzing lobstermen herself, enjoyed employing game theory to try to predict the behaviour of people faced with limited resources. In her Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis at Indiana University—set up with her husband Vincent, a political scientist, in 1973—her students were given shares in a national common. When they discussed what they should do before they did it, their rate of return from their "investments" more than doubled. Her later, and more famous, work focused on how humans interact with [ecosystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecosystem "Ecosystem") to maintain long-term sustainable resource yields. Common pool resources include many forests, fisheries, oil fields, grazing lands, and irrigation systems. She conducted her field studies on the management of pasture by locals in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") and irrigation systems management in villages of western [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") (e.g., [Dang Deukhuri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dang_Deukhuri_District "Dang Deukhuri District")). Her work has considered how societies have developed diverse [institutional arrangements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institution "Institution") for [managing natural resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_resource_management "Natural resource management") and avoiding [ecosystem collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecosystem_collapse "Ecosystem collapse") in many cases, even though some arrangements have failed to prevent resource exhaustion. Her work emphasized the multifaceted nature of human–ecosystem interaction and argues against any singular "panacea" for individual [social-ecological system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_ecological_model "Social ecological model") problems.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-36)

### "Design principles illustrated by long-enduring CPR (Common Pool Resource) institutions"

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: \"Design principles illustrated by long-enduring CPR (Common Pool Resource) institutions\"")]

In _Governing the Commons_, Ostrom summarized eight design principles that were present in the sustainable common pool resource institutions she studied:[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-38)

> 1.   Clearly defined boundaries: Individuals or households who have rights to withdraw resource units from the CPR must be clearly defined, as must the boundaries of the CPR itself.
> 2.   Congruence between appropriation and provision rules and local conditions: Appropriation rules restricting time, place, technology, and/or quantity of resource units are related to local labor, material, and/or money.
> 3.   Collective-choice arrangements: Most individuals affected by the operational rules can participate in modifying the operational rules.
> 4.   Monitoring: Monitors, who actively audit CPR conditions and appropriator behavior, are accountable to the appropriators or are the appropriators.
> 5.   Graduated sanctions: Appropriators who violate operational rules are likely to be assessed graduated sanctions (depending on the seriousness and context of the offense) by other appropriators, by officials accountable to these appropriators, or by both.
> 6.   Conflict-resolution mechanisms: Appropriators and their officials have rapid access to low-cost local arenas to resolve conflicts among appropriators or between appropriators and officials.
> 7.   Minimal recognition of rights to organize: The rights of appropriators to devise their own institutions are not challenged by external governmental authorities.
> 
> 
> _For CPRs that are parts of larger systems:_
> 
> 
> 
> 1.   Nested enterprises: Appropriation, provision, monitoring, enforcement, conflict resolution, and governance activities are organized in multiple layers of nested enterprises.

These principles have since been slightly modified and expanded to include a number of additional variables believed to affect the success of [self-organized governance systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-organized#Self-organization_in_human_society "Self-organized"), including effective communication, [internal trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trust_(social_sciences) "Trust (social sciences)") and [reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_(cultural_anthropology) "Reciprocity (cultural anthropology)"), and the nature of the resource system as a whole.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-39)

Ostrom and her many co-researchers have developed a comprehensive "[Social-Ecological Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socio-ecological_system "Socio-ecological system") (SES) framework", within which much of the still-evolving theory of common-pool resources and collective [self-governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-governance "Self-governance") is now located.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-40)

### Environmental protection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Environmental protection")]

According to the [Norwegian Institute for Urban and Regional Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Institute_for_Urban_and_Regional_Research "Norwegian Institute for Urban and Regional Research"), "Ostrom cautioned against single governmental units at global level to solve the collective action problem of coordinating work against [environmental destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_destruction "Environmental destruction"). Partly, this is due to their complexity, and partly to the diversity of actors involved. Her proposal was that of a polycentric approach, where key management decisions should be made as close to the scene of events and the actors involved as possible." Ostrom helped disprove the idea held by economists that natural resources would be over-used and destroyed in the long run. Elinor Ostrom disproved this idea by conducting field studies on how people in small, local communities manage shared natural resources, such as pastures, fishing waters in Maine and Indonesia, and forests in Nepal. She showed that when natural resources are jointly managed by their users, in time, rules are established for how these are to be cared for and used in a way that is both economically and ecologically sustainable.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-41)

### Ostrom's law

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Ostrom's law")]

**Ostrom's law** is an [adage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adage "Adage") that represents how Elinor Ostrom's works in [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") challenge previous theoretical frameworks and assumptions about [property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property "Property"), especially the [commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commons "Commons"). Ostrom's detailed analyses of functional examples of the commons create an alternative view of the arrangement of [resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resources "Resources") that are both practically and theoretically possible. This [eponymous law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous_law "Eponymous law") is stated succinctly by Lee Anne Fennell as:

> A resource arrangement that works in practice can work in theory.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-42)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

After college, Ostrom married a classmate, Charles Scott, and worked at [General Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Radio "General Radio") in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), while Scott attended [Harvard Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Law_School "Harvard Law School").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Leonard-7) They divorced several years later when Ostrom began contemplating a Ph.D.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Leonard-7)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Harford-43)

Her postgraduate seminar was led by [Vincent Ostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Ostrom "Vincent Ostrom"), an associate professor of political science, 14 years her senior, whom she married in 1963. This marked the beginning of a lifelong partnership of "love and contestation," as Ostrom put it in her dedication to her seminal 1990 book, _Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action._[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:1-20)

### Nobel Prize in Economics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Nobel Prize in Economics")]

In 2009, Ostrom became the first woman to receive the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences"). The [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") cited Ostrom "for her analysis of economic governance", saying her work had demonstrated how [common property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_property "Common property") could be successfully managed by groups using it. Ostrom and [Oliver E. Williamson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_E._Williamson "Oliver E. Williamson") shared the 10-million [Swedish kronor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona") (€990,000; $1.44 million) prize for their separate work in [economic governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_governance "Economic governance").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-bbc_20091012_ostromprize-52) As she had done with previous monetary prizes, Ostrom donated her award to the Workshop she helped to found.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Wall-9)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Arrow-53)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Group_Photo_%284171912803%29.jpg/250px-Group_Photo_%284171912803%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Group_Photo_(4171912803).jpg)

Elinor Ostrom with the other 2009 Nobel laureates

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said Ostrom's "research brought this topic from the fringe to the forefront of scientific attention...by showing how common resources—forests, [fisheries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisheries "Fisheries"), [oil fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_fields "Oil fields") or [grazing lands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazing "Grazing")—can be managed successfully by the people who use them rather than by governments or private companies". Ostrom's work in this regard challenged [conventional wisdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventional_wisdom "Conventional wisdom"), showing that common resources can be successfully managed without [government regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_regulation "Government regulation") or [privatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization "Privatization").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-NYTObit-54)

In awarding Ostrom the Nobel Prize for the Analysis of Economic Governance, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences noted that her work "teaches us novel lessons about the deep mechanisms that sustain cooperation in human societies." Even if Ostrom's selection (along with co-recipient Oliver Williamson of the University of California, Berkeley) seemed odd to some, others saw it as an appropriate reaction to free-market inefficiencies highlighted by the 2008 financial crisis.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-:1-20)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elinor_Ostrom&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Death")]

Ostrom was diagnosed with [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") in October 2011.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-56) During the final year of her life, she continued to write and lecture, giving the [Hayek Lecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayek_Lecture "Hayek Lecture") at the [Institute of Economic Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Economic_Affairs "Institute of Economic Affairs") just eleven weeks before her death.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Wall-9) She died at 6:40 a.m. Tuesday, June 12, 2012, at IU Health Bloomington Hospital at the age of 78.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-auto-28) On the day of her death, she published her last article, "Green from the Grassroots," in [Project Syndicate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Syndicate "Project Syndicate").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-58)[Indiana University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_University "Indiana University") president [Michael McRobbie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_McRobbie "Michael McRobbie") wrote: "Indiana University has lost an irreplaceable and magnificent treasure with the passing of Elinor Ostrom".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-59) Her Indiana colleague Michael McGinnis commented after her death that Ostrom donated her share of the $1.4 million Nobel award money to the Workshop—the biggest, by far, of several academic prizes with monetary awards that the Ostroms had given to the center over the years.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-Arrow_13135%E2%80%9313136-24) Her husband Vincent died 17 days later from complications related to cancer. He was 92.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elinor_Ostrom#cite_note-60)

# James E. Meade

## Facts

![Image 1: James E. Meade](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1)

Photo from the Nobel Foundation archive.

James E. Meade  
 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1977

Born: 23 June 1907, Swanage, United Kingdom

Died: 22 December 1995, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Affiliation at the time of the award: University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Prize motivation: “for their pathbreaking contribution to the theory of international trade and international capital movements”

Prize share: 1/2

### Life

James Meade was born in Bath, UK. He was educated at Malvern College and Oriel College at Oxford, where he earned first-class honors in 1928. He served as a war economist during WWII and was the leading economist in the Labor government 1946-47, after which he took up professorship at London School of Economics (1947-57) and Cambridge (1957-67).

### Work

In his major work The Theory of International Economic Policy (1951/55), James Meade demonstrated the effects of economic policy on foreign trade and penetrated the problems of stabilization policies in “open” economies. Open economies are defined as those that are greatly dependent on foreign trade. These achievements made Meade a pioneer in the field of international macro-theory and international economic policy.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Nobel2008Economics_news_conference1.jpg/250px-Nobel2008Economics_news_conference1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobel2008Economics_news_conference1.jpg)

The announcement of the 2008 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in Nobel Prize Press Conference. The laureate of the Prize was [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman").

The **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences**, officially the **Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-3) ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Sveriges riksbanks pris i ekonomisk vetenskap till Alfred Nobels minne_), commonly referred to as the **Nobel Prize in Economics**, is an award in the field of [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeSelectionProcess-4)

The first Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded in 1969 to [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch") and [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-Winners1969-5) Each recipient receives a [medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma") and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-6) In 1969, Frisch and Tinbergen were given a combined 375,000 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), which is equivalent to 2,871,041 SEK in December 2007. The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-7)

As of the awarding of the 2023 prize, 55 Prizes in Economic Sciences have been given to 93 individuals.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-NobelLaureatesList-8) As of October 2023, the department of economics with the most affiliated [laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate") in economic sciences is the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_Memorial_Prize_laureates_in_Economic_Sciences#cite_note-10) with 16 affiliated laureates. As of 2023, the institutions with the most [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") (or equivalent) graduates who went on to receive the prize are Harvard University and MIT (13 each), followed by the University of Chicago (10). As of 2024, the institutions with the most affiliated faculty at the time of the award are the University of Chicago (15), followed by MIT (10), then by Princeton University and Harvard University (8 each).

# James E. Meade

## Facts

![Image 1: James E. Meade](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1)

Photo from the Nobel Foundation archive.

James E. Meade  
 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1977

Born: 23 June 1907, Swanage, United Kingdom

Died: 22 December 1995, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Affiliation at the time of the award: University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Prize motivation: “for their pathbreaking contribution to the theory of international trade and international capital movements”

Prize share: 1/2

### Life

James Meade was born in Bath, UK. He was educated at Malvern College and Oriel College at Oxford, where he earned first-class honors in 1928. He served as a war economist during WWII and was the leading economist in the Labor government 1946-47, after which he took up professorship at London School of Economics (1947-57) and Cambridge (1957-67).

### Work

In his major work The Theory of International Economic Policy (1951/55), James Meade demonstrated the effects of economic policy on foreign trade and penetrated the problems of stabilization policies in “open” economies. Open economies are defined as those that are greatly dependent on foreign trade. These achievements made Meade a pioneer in the field of international macro-theory and international economic policy.
